notes:
I've put together notes on Job 25 for all six verses. Most of the material comes from the older commentaries on biblehub.com and studylight.org, plus Guzik on enduringword.com. Here's what I couldn't find:

- **Wesley:** his own notes on chapter 25 weren't on the part of the page I could read.
- **Lutheran and Anglican:** I found no teachers from these traditions.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Popular modern teaching:** no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material.

**Overview (whole chapter)**
- This is the friends' last speech. It is so short because the debate is running out of steam: Job has silenced them even if he hasn't convinced them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/
- Bildad doesn't answer Job's point that the wicked often prosper. He goes back to two familiar themes: God's might (vv. 2–3) and the sinfulness of all people. He does avoid Eliphaz's reckless charges. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-25.html
- Matthew Henry finds two lessons in it: think highly of God and humbly of ourselves. Bildad applies them wrongly to Job, but they are still good lessons. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_025.cfm

**v. 1:** Ellicott says Bildad makes no real reply. He falls back on a position Eliphaz had already taken twice, that no one can be just before God, and so implies Job is wrong to keep claiming he is righteous. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-1.htm
- Barnes thinks Job's appeal to the facts was decisive. In his view the Holy Spirit recorded the debate partly to show that the friends' theory of how God governs was false. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-1.htm
- *Modern scholarship:* Guzik quotes Smick saying most modern scholars make the speech longer by adding 26:5–14. Smick sees no good reason to do this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/

**v. 2:** "Dominion and awe" means God has the right to rule and deserves reverence. Barnes says "high places" means the heavens, where God keeps peace among the heavenly hosts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-2.html
- Matthew Henry says the angels never quarrel with God or with each other. He links this to the angels announcing peace on earth (Luke 2:14). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_025.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the verse may mean God keeps peace among heavenly beings. It may also hint at a time when peace was broken (a "war in heaven") and God had to restore it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-25.html
- The Cambridge Bible thinks the picture may start with God calming a storm, then widen to old stories of conflict among the heavenly hosts. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown sees a hint of the gospel here (Col 1:20). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-2.htm

**v. 3:** Poole (quoted by Guzik) says God's "armies" are angels, stars and other creatures that all obey him, so it is foolish to quarrel with him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/
- The Pulpit Commentary points to Daniel 7:10 and similar verses for the countless angels. It reads "his light" as the light every creature shines with, reflected from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-25.html
- Keil and Delitzsch translate it differently: "whom doth not His light surpass?" In other words, God's light outshines every being of light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-4.htm
- Matthew Henry reads the light as God's goodness and providence, which reach everyone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Job/Job_025.cfm

**v. 4:** Guzik says this was not actually in dispute, because Job had said the same thing (9:2). Bildad's aim seems to be to get Job to admit he is a sinner like everyone else. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/
- Barnes calls the saying true but beside the point, since Job had said the same himself (14:4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-4.htm
- Constable says the question isn't answered in Job. The answer came later, in the good news of God's grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-25.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the verse implies no one is justified by works, only by grace through faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-25.html

*Where the traditions differ.* They all agree on the basic point. They differ in how they explain the answer:
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** Job wanted his *cause* cleared, not his *person* justified, since he trusted his living Redeemer for that. Gill describes justification in three stages: in God's court, in the believer's conscience when they believe, and publicly at the day of judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-4.htm
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** a sinner is justified by faith in Christ's sacrifice. Clarke adds that a believer "convinced of indwelling sin" can also be sanctified, that is, cleansed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-4.html
- **Matthew Henry (Reformed):** he separates two problems. Our actual sins leave us guilty before God's justice, and the corruption we are born with makes us offensive to his holiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-4.html
- **Benson (Methodist):** following Poole, he stresses that the Hebrew word for man (*enosh*) means "miserable man." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/job-25.html
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** no one can be justified with God apart from what Jesus Christ has done. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-4.html

**v. 5:** Bildad means that even the brightest parts of creation fall short of God's glory. Clarke can't see the fallen angels in the word "stars." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/
- Clarke also guesses the speech was given at night, which would explain why the sun isn't mentioned. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/job-25.html
- Coffman disagrees with Bildad: the stars *are* pure in God's sight. He takes this as an example of the friends not speaking rightly of God (42:7). https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/job-25.html

**v. 6:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes two different Hebrew words. The first is a worm bred in rot (pointing to corruption), the second a crawling worm (pointing to weakness). Benson says "son of man" makes the point true even of the greatest people, and marvels that God takes such worms into fellowship with himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/25-6.htm
- Matthew Henry points to Christ's own words in Psalm 22:6: "I am a worm, and no man." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-6.html
- The Pulpit Commentary calls it a truism that misses the point. Job never claimed to be sinless, only that his sins didn't explain his suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-25.html
- Guzik quotes Smick: unlike Paul in Romans 1–3, Bildad offers no mercy. He also quotes Andersen calling this a "disgusting and hopeless note" to end on. He notes the irony that these "maggots" were judging a fellow maggot. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-25/
- A Pulpit homily warns that it's possible to abuse this idea, and that calling yourself "a worm" can hide pride. https://biblehub.com/sermons/job/25-6.htm
- *Modern scholarship:* the NET note says "maggot" and "worm" describe humanity at its lowest and most shameful. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=job&chapter=25&verse=6
- *Old versions:* Clarke reports that most ancient versions read "man is corruption." The Douay-Rheims has "rottenness." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/25-6.html | https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/job/25-6.html
